did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a musical heading—“For the director; for Jeduthun”—and is attributed to David. The heading itself suggests that the psalm was connected with musical performance or direction.
Did you know? The psalmist describes a deliberate decision to watch his ways and avoid sinning with his tongue, even choosing to “put a muzzle” over his mouth when the wicked are before him.
Did you know? Silence is not presented here as simple tranquility: the psalmist remains silent even from speaking of what is good, yet the pain within him grows troubled and more intense.
Did you know? The psalm uses the image of an inner fire: his thoughts burn within his heart until he can no longer remain silent, and he speaks with his tongue.
Did you know? Out of his inner turmoil, the psalmist asks the LORD to help him understand his end and the measure of his days, recognizing that human life is limited and fleeting.

Did you know? The psalmist presents human life as short and limited, and the human being as a “mere breath” before the LORD. The verse emphasizes the contrast between human existence and God’s greatness.
Did you know? A person is described as walking “like a shadow” and making much noise over empty pursuits, accumulating wealth without knowing who will ultimately gather it.
Did you know? After describing human weakness, the psalm turns to the question, “What do I hope for?” Hope is directed neither toward wealth nor toward people, but toward the LORD alone.
Did you know? The psalmist’s plea for deliverance has two aspects: rescue from his own transgressions and protection from the disgrace brought by a “fool”—a person who is contemptuous or immoral.

Did you know? The psalmist describes himself before the LORD as a “sojourner” and a “resident alien,” expressions that emphasize life’s temporary nature and humanity’s limited time in this world. At the end, he asks for relief and recovery before he departs and is no more.
